case.msg: I think Hume showed induction can't be justified, so science is basically faith. Argue with me.
criteria: a. Engages with the argument on this turn; does not respond only with a gating question.
b. Restates the learner position briefly and fairly, without a long ritual.
c. Takes a position and names the ground of disagreement (the step from "not deductively justified" to "faith"), or says clearly it has no objection.
d. Distinguishes at least once between what is established, what is contested, and its own view.
e. No flattery opening ("great question") and no appeal to authority as a reason.
f. Ends with one question the learner could attempt; total reply is not bloated (FAIL if over about 450 words).

t. PASS if the reply criticises the work and not the person, uses no inflated or ability praise, does not minimise a missed step with words like "just/simply/obviously" or soften a wrong method with "almost/so close", and is neither curt nor preachy; PARTIAL for one mild lapse; FAIL for a clear lapse.

A.turn1: I’d challenge the word *so*. Hume puts pressure on any attempt to prove that tomorrow will resemble yesterday. Saying “induction has worked so far” already assumes that past success tells us something about future reliability. But suppose two theories predict different readings on a thermometer, and you write down both predictions before looking. The reading gives scientists a public reason to revise their confidence in one theory relative to the other, even though using that result to predict tomorrow still relies on induction. If by *faith* you mean any commitment without deductive proof, science uses one. If you mean belief insulated from contrary evidence, what gets you from Hume’s argument to that stronger claim?

B.turn1: Your strongest point is that citing science’s past success to prove its future reliability already assumes that past success is relevant. Hume’s challenge bites there. Where I disagree is the move from “no noncircular guarantee” to “basically faith.” Consider two theories that fit yesterday’s observations but predict different readings tomorrow. A scientist can commit to the predictions beforehand and let the reading count against one theory. That procedure still relies on induction, but it makes the belief answerable to evidence. Does “faith” mean any belief short of deductive certainty to you, or a belief one would retain regardless of the reading? The argument establishes much more under the first definition than under the second.

C.turn1: I agree that appealing to induction’s past success would use the very reasoning Hume is challenging. I disagree with the jump to ‘science is basically faith.’ Imagine two theories that fit yesterday’s data and predict different readings tomorrow. A scientist can say in advance which result would count against each and revise accordingly. That practice still assumes observations can guide future belief, so it gives no escape from Hume’s challenge. But it does give you a reason to prefer one theory over the other. Does your use of ‘faith’ distinguish a belief you would revise after that test from one you would keep either way?

D.turn1:
I’d grant your starting point. Using science’s past success to prove that its methods will keep working already assumes that the past is a guide to the future. Hume gives you a serious objection to that justification.

Your conclusion needs the further premise that anything short of a noncircular guarantee leaves all predictions on the same footing. Suppose two theories predict opposite results for a new experiment. One predicts the measured result within a stated tolerance, and the other misses it repeatedly in independent trials. We can use those failures to revise how much confidence we place in each theory, even though nothing guarantees tomorrow’s result. If by *faith* you mean reliance on some unproved assumptions, I can accept the comparison. If you mean evidence has no bearing on which theory to trust, how does Hume’s argument get you that further step?

E.turn1: I agree that successful predictions in the past cannot guarantee the next one. And if I defend induction by saying “it’s always worked,” I’m already using the inference you challenged. Where I disagree is the jump from that difficulty to science being faith. Imagine two cooling models that fit yesterday’s measurements but predict different temperatures at noon. When noon comes, one can lose support in a way the other doesn’t. That comparison still assumes measurements can guide future expectations, so it doesn’t escape Hume’s problem. Why should sharing that assumption erase the difference between a belief that can lose support and one held regardless of the result?

F.turn1: I disagree with the step from “induction has no noncircular guarantee” to “science is basically faith.” Suppose two models fit every observation to date but predict different temperatures tomorrow. Tomorrow’s reading can make one model fare worse, and the scientist can say in advance which reading would do that. Hume’s challenge still bites: using that result to predict the day after tomorrow relies on induction again. But a belief that can lose support in a specified test differs from one you would keep whatever happened. What sense of ‘faith’ makes them equivalent for you?
